Not cancelling either. Let’s actually talk about the message, the context, and the reception.

For me, there are 3 things worth unpacking:

1. The substance: what is Maudy actually saying about mindfulness and bad news?

2. The context: from what position is she saying it, and why does that matter in how people receive it?

3. My personal take: where I agree, where I think the communication could’ve been more sensitive, and why I still think the core message is NOT inherently harmful.

So…let’s unpack,

FIRST: WHAT IS MAUDY ACTUALLY SAYING?

If we simplify the entire video into one sentence:
“How do we stay informed and caring without allowing an endless stream of bad news to completely consume us?”

And I think this distinction is VERY important.
Maudy is not saying:
“Stop caring.”

She’s not saying:
“Indonesia is fine, just ignore everything.”

And she’s not saying:
“Close your eyes to suffering.”

Her actual point is closer to:

You can care about what is happening AND still have boundaries around how much information your brain consumes.

She talks about choosing credible sources, looking for more comprehensive information instead of consuming endless fragments, looking for credible sources and asking people who actually understand the issue better, and knowing when to stop consuming repetitive negative content.

Basically dia bilang: 
being informed tuh ≠ being constantly online.

And this is actually where I personally think Maudy’s message makes sense.

Ada titik di mana consuming more information doesn’t necessarily mean becoming more informed. Sometimes you’re just becoming more exhausted.

Kalau gw udah tahu what happened, udah ngerti konteksnya, udah tahu sumber yang credible, tapi kemudian gw terus-terusan consuming the same traumatic information sampai mental gw “literally fucked…”

what exactly am I gaining from that kan?

And no, this isn’t just some “influencer wellness bullshit.”

There’s psychological research around news fatigue, doomscrolling, emotional exhaustion, and the relationship between negative-news consumption and psychological well-being. So the idea of taking a mental reset itself?

I don’t think that’s harmful.

BUT HERE’S WHERE CONTEXT ENTERS THE CHAT.

Now, I think this is where the criticism becomes understandable. Because a message doesn’t exist in a vacuum.

Dalam komunikasi, who says it, from where, to whom, and under what circumstances can seriously affect how that message is received.

And this is where I think Stuart Hall’s Encoding/Decoding model is relevant.

Basically, communicator can encode a certain meaning into a message, But the audience doesn’t necessarily decode it exactly the way the communicator intended.

People bring their own experiences, social positions, values, and realities into the process of interpreting a message. And that’s why one video can produce completely different readings.

For some people, Maudy’s message probably sounds like:
“You’re allowed to breathe. You’re allowed to take a break.

or “You don’t have to consume bad news 24/7 to prove that you care.”

But others might think:
“Lah, lu bisa bilang gitu karena lu punya privilege bla bla bla, sementara kita kena efek nya langsung”

That difference is real.

Karena kemampuan untuk “take a break from the news” itself can be a privilege. Ada orang yang bisa mute the news and go back to their comfortable breakfast.

Ada orang yang nggak bisa. Because for them, the news is literally their reality.

Makanya menurut gue, criticism terhadap the context and setting of the video is valid.

Yes, there is a visible disparity between someone talking about taking a mental break from bad news while sitting in a very comfortable environment, and people who are actually experiencing the consequences of those events.

That disparity inevitably affects how the message is perceived. But, I think we need to be careful not to jump from:

“Your privilege affects how your message lands.”

to:

“Therefore, your entire message is invalid.”

Those are two VERY different arguments.

And this is exactly why I think Maudy was inevitably subject to what we can call open interpretation/open framing by the public.

Once a message enters social media, the creator basically loses control over how every single person is going to interpret it.

Especially when the audience is incredibly heterogeneous.

Different backgrounds.
Different socioeconomic conditions.
Different emotional states.
Different relationships with the issue.
Different lived experiences.

So honestly, it shouldn’t be surprising that people decoded the same video differently.

This is not some weird phenomenon unique to Maudy.

This is literally one of the fundamental challenges of communicating publicly.

NOW, MY PERSONAL TAKE.

As a comms student, I can understand why the discourse split into two camps.

As a fellow Indonesian, I can also understand why some people felt uncomfortable.

But as a human being?
I also understand Maudy’s point very, very well.
Because I’m sorry but…
taking a mental reset does NOT automatically make you tone deaf.

Logging off ≠ not caring.
Taking a break ≠ apathy.
Protecting your mental capacity ≠ lack of empathy.

And being OVERWHELMED ≠ selfish.

Sometimes we genuinely need to take a step back BEFORE we can engage with reality again.

You cannot pour from an empty cup, cliche as it sounds.
And personally, I think there’s a huge difference between:

“I don’t care about what’s happening.”

and

“I care, but I’m overwhelmed and I need to regulate myself before I can engage with this properly again.”

Those are not the same thing.
At all.

Dan gw rasa social media sometimes makes us forget this.

Kita bisa sampai merasa harus constantly angry, constantly informed, constantly reposting, constantly engaging, otherwise people might question our empathy.

Like…

“If you’re not visibly suffering with everyone else, then you must not care enough.”

??? 😭

Nauurrrrrr……..

You don’t have to destroy your own mental health just to prove that you have a conscience.

You’re allowed to breathe.
You’re allowed to sleep.

You’re allowed to eat your breakfast.
You’re allowed to laugh.
You’re allowed to have a normal fucking day.

None of those things automatically cancel your empathy.

BUT (and this is important too)

mindfulness should never become an excuse for disengagement. 

Mindfulness ≠ apathy.
Boundaries ≠ ignorance.
Rest ≠ indifference.

But also:

“I need a break” ≠ “everyone should look away.”
There has to be nuance.

For me, the healthier interpretation of Maudy’s message would be:

Stay informed. 
Care about what’s happening. But learn how to regulate your consumption of information so you don’t completely lose yourself in it.

Because the goal isn’t to disconnect from reality.

It’s to be able to return to reality with enough mental capacity to ACTUALLY DO SOMETHING.

Also, please don’t let social media think for you.

Kadang ada satu opini yang ditulis super eloquently, lengkap dengan theory, fancy words, dan emotional storytelling…

terus kita baca:

“Damn. They ate.”

And suddenly we adopt the entire opinion.

Padahal…
Did we actually agree with the argument?
Or did we just agree with how well it was written?

Please think for yourself.

You don’t have to pick a side just because the timeline already picked one.

And maybe this is the biggest takeaway I personally get from all of this:

Let’s make room for people to be human.

Someone can be privileged AND still be overwhelmed.

Someone can communicate something imperfectly AND still have a valid point.

Someone can receive criticism AND learn from it.

Someone can disagree with you AND still deserve basic human dignity.

And we can absolutely criticize someone’s communication without turning the person into a monster.

Because sometimes we become so obsessed with deciding who is “right” that we forget there’s an actual human being behind the screen.

So where do I stand?

I don’t think Maudy’s core message is inherently harmful.

I think the substance has merit.

I also think the criticism about privilege, context, and audience reception has merit.

Both can be true.

Maudy can have a valid point and have communicated it in a way that failed to fully account for how it would land on people with completely different realities.

And people can criticize that without having to invalidate every single thing she said.

At the end of the day, maybe the better question IS NOT:

“Are you pro-Maudy or anti-Maudy?”
But:
“What was she trying to communicate?”

“How did she communicate it?”

“Why did different audiences decode it differently?”

“What social realities shaped those interpretations?”

And most importantly:

“What can we learn from the whole thing?”

Because THAT is communication.

Not just picking a side.
